title: Optional Module A: Communicating through Traditional Media
summary: People without electricity, literacy and basic infrastructure cannot easily use television, newspapers or radio, but traditional media need only space to perform (a street play in front of a tea stall or under a tree), so they are flexible, live and natural. For communication to reach a common person it must be simple and free from language barriers; traditional media meet this. They are rich in variety, readily available and economically viable, enjoyed by men and women of all ages, win the confidence of rural masses because they are live and create a 'face-to-face situation'. They are free from advertisements, so they are need-based and purposeful; entertainment is always part of them, blended with education, and they create no false desires or expectations.

Festivals in villages have performances, games, motifs and paintings that give relaxation, entertainment and team spirit; communication flows in them in an intimate, personal way. Traditional media are part of a community's way of life and bring development issues in on its own terms; they played a significant role in the freedom movement and have conveyed messages on population, health and hygiene through ritualistic dances, religious songs and mythology-based rural plays. Flexibility is the most important factor deciding the viability of a traditional medium. There are no cross-cultural hurdles as performances and fine arts need no language. A market, festival, ritual, village fair, social gathering or celebration are situations where traditional communication takes place. Government bodies such as the Song and Drama Division, educational institutions and NGOs use street plays, songs and dances, whose primary appeal is to emotion rather than intellect.

Traditional media can create awareness and sensitise people on social issues, especially sensitive health issues like HIV/AIDS where face-to-face communication is not suitable (a puppet show); they spread family planning and polio immunisation messages. A ballad is a poem usually set to music, often a story told as a song; ballads are called 'bullets' because of their power; used for environment, energy conservation and dowry, often humorous with rhythmic play of words. Street theatre combines traditional theatre forms and techniques; its flexibility lets short plays be staged anywhere, with songs, drama and music on child labour, environment, health and women. While using traditional media for social messages the original form must not be changed; there is a risk of distorting the forms.

Sustainability: viewers contribute money after performances to keep artists and art alive. Many forms are disappearing as performers change professions because of television and lack of financial support; they are not taught in schools and oral traditions have no written documentation. We can help by viewing, writing, talking and learning about them. The government has established bodies such as the Song and Drama Division, Sangeet Natak Akademi, Lalit Kala Academy and Directorate of Audio-Visual Publicity for their revival and survival. The challenge is to save the few traditional forms from eroding and revive the older forms for the future.
mcqA: Which government body works for the revival and survival of traditional media?
Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade
Which traditional media form can be used to create awareness on health issues where face-to-face communication is not easy?
Which of the following is an essential characteristic of communication to reach a common person?
It must be free from language barriers
What is the reason for traditional media performers to leave their creative art?
Which of the following is a requirement of traditional media?
poem set to music, often a story told in song
The traditional media which combines songs, drama and music includes —

objA: State true or false: (i) Traditional media is very useful to deal with sensitive issues of health. (ii) A market, festival, ritual or village fair are situations where traditional communication takes place.
Fill in the blanks: Various governmental bodies like ______ and ______ division use traditional media for creating awareness.
Sangeet Natak Akademi (Song and Drama); Song and Drama.
Fill in the blanks: There is always a risk of ______ the forms of traditional media while using them for conveying messages on ______ issues.
Fill in the blanks: A ballad is a ______ usually set to music and is often told in the form of a ______.
Fill in the blanks: Ram Lila, the story of ______, is celebrated and performed all over ______ India.
State true or false: Folk theatre is an example of traditional media; traditional media needs advanced technology.
Name any two government bodies promoting traditional media.
Song and Drama Division and Sangeet Natak Akademi (also Lalit Kala Academy).
vsaA: Explain street theatre and its application.
Street theatre combines traditional theatre forms and can be staged anywhere; it uses songs, drama and music to spread messages on child labour, environment, health and women.
Write a short note on any one: (i) Demonstrations (ii) Puppetry.

Demonstrations help transfer knowledge and encourage farmers to try new ideas, with story telling and plays at weekly markets. Puppetry combines entertainment with education and treats sensitive topics such as HIV/AIDS.
List the situations where traditional communication takes place.
Markets, festivals, rituals, village fairs, social gatherings and celebrations.
Why is traditional media useful to deal with sensitive health issues?
Face-to-face communication is not suitable, but a puppet show or play can explain the issue conveniently and effectively.
A poem usually set to music, often a story told as a song; used for messages on environment or dowry.
laA: Why do we consider traditional media as the most effective tool for cross-cultural communication? Give example.
Performances and fine arts need no language, so they communicate solidarity and friendship through non-verbal communication; e.g. folk dance or a puppet show understood across regions.
Explain the role of traditional media in development communication.

They carry messages on health, polio, family planning, education and environment in the people's own forms such as street theatre, ballads and puppetry, face to face and without language barriers, using government bodies like the Song and Drama Division.
Discuss the problems faced by traditional media for their survival and how they can be preserved.

Performers leave due to television and lack of financial support, forms are not taught and have no written documentation; support through viewing, learning, and government bodies like Sangeet Natak Akademi and Song and Drama Division can preserve them.
